passage: Noor was sitting behind Sarita in science on Wednesday when the teacher said the model volcano's label was hard to read and the crater too small. Sarita spun around in her chair. "The glue was old! Also Riya knocked it! Also nobody told us the size!" The teacher waited until she stopped, then moved on. Sarita sat with her arms folded until the bell. But at lunch, Noor saw her outside the lab with a marker, quietly rewriting the label in bigger letters. She widened the crater with her thumbs. Noor kept walking, and pretended not to have seen anything.

qa.q: What did the teacher say was wrong with the volcano model?
qa.a: The teacher said the label was hard to read and the crater was too small.

qa.q: What does Sarita's list of excuses suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt stung and proud, and wanted to defend herself before she could take in the feedback.

qa.q: What could Sarita try next time she gets feedback like this?
qa.a: She could listen to the whole comment and write it down before answering, then decide privately what to change.

qa.q: Why might Noor pretend not to have seen Sarita fixing the label?
qa.a: Noor seems to see that Sarita is quietly using the feedback and wants to spare her pride, so saying nothing lets her keep her dignity.

grounding: Shows a teenager listing excuses when critiqued but privately using the useful part later, with a classmate observing.

passage:
Monday. Vidya ma'am handed back Dhruv's essay with a line under the first paragraph: "Too long. Start at your second sentence." Dhruv said the printer had jammed, exams were on, and the topic was too wide anyway. Vidya ma'am let him finish and said only, "Think about it."
Tuesday night. At his desk, Dhruv opened the file and looked at the first paragraph for a long minute. He deleted the opening sentence and began at the second.
The next Monday, Vidya ma'am read the new version and said, "This is much clearer." Dhruv shrugged. "I was going to change it anyway."

qa.q: What did Vidya ma'am write under the first paragraph of Dhruv's essay?
qa.a: She wrote "Too long. Start at your second sentence."

qa.q: What did Dhruv's remark "I was going to change it anyway" show he was feeling?
qa.a: It showed his pride, since he wanted to keep the feeling that the change was his own idea instead of admitting he had taken the advice.

qa.q: What turning point happened on Tuesday night?
qa.a: Dhruv opened the file alone, looked at the first paragraph and started at the second sentence, using the feedback once no one was watching.

qa.q: How might Vidya ma'am see Dhruv's excuses on Monday?
qa.a: She lets him finish and says only "Think about it," which suggests she sees the excuses as pride and trusts him to use the point later.

grounding: Shows a teenager defensive on the first day and quietly using the feedback in private on later days.

passage:
Dear Diary, Sunday.
Baljeet bhaiya watched my bowling today and said my front arm drops too early. Before he'd even finished, I said the ball was wet, my shoes were slipping, and he doesn't even bowl pace so what does he know. He just shrugged and walked off.
I was so annoyed. I'm the best bowler in my school team!
But tonight, alone in the lane with a tennis ball, I tried keeping my front arm up longer. The ball went straighter. Five out of six on the stump. I'm not telling bhaiya. At least not yet.
Maybe I was angry because he was right.
Gurpreet

qa.q: What did Baljeet bhaiya say about Gurpreet's bowling?
qa.a: He said the front arm drops too early.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet react with excuses?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt annoyed and proud, hearing the feedback as an attack, being the best bowler in the school team.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet do later, and what does it show?
qa.a: Gurpreet quietly practised keeping the front arm up and bowled straighter, showing the reaction was about pride, not disagreement.

qa.q: How might Baljeet bhaiya feel when Gurpreet argued?
qa.a: He seemed unbothered or a bit resigned, shrugging and walking off without pushing the point.

grounding: A diary shows a teenager hearing feedback as an attack and listing excuses, then quietly using it later.

passage: In the small government school in a Kerala village, Chaitanya, sixteen, gave a speech for the district elocution contest. His teacher, Thomas sir, said, "Good voice. But you speak too fast, and your ending is weak." Before Thomas sir had finished, Chaitanya was talking. "The mic was bad. And I only practised twice because of exams. And the judges like fast speakers." Thomas sir listened, nodded and said, "Think about it." That evening, walking by the paddy fields, Chaitanya practised the speech again, slower. He rewrote the ending by lamplight. At the contest, he spoke calmly and finished strong. Afterwards he told Thomas sir, "You were right," looking at his shoes.

qa.q: Which contest was Chaitanya's speech for?
qa.a: The district elocution contest.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling when he started listing excuses?
qa.a: He felt defensive and stung in his pride, hearing the feedback as an attack.

qa.q: What did Thomas sir do well when Chaitanya argued?
qa.a: He listened and simply said to think about it, leaving room for Chaitanya to use the feedback privately.

qa.q: How might Thomas sir feel hearing "You were right"?
qa.a: Thomas sir would likely feel quietly pleased and warm, seeing that the feedback had been used despite the first reaction.

grounding: Shows a teenager defending himself against feedback with excuses, then quietly using it in private.

passage: "The middle drags," Noa said, tapping page four, "and your characters talk like my parents." They were on the steps outside school in Valencia, sharing a bag of sunflower seeds, the short-film script between them. Alejandro felt his face go hot. "You read it too fast. The slow part's on purpose. And I wrote it after football, so obviously—" He heard himself listing reasons and couldn't stop. Noa shrugged. "Okay. Just saying." At home he threw the script on the bed and ignored it through dinner. At eleven he opened page four, read it aloud, and winced. He deleted the whole bus-stop scene and rewrote two lines so they sounded like actual teenagers. The next morning he handed Noa the new version without a word. Noa read it and grinned.

qa.q: Which scene did Alejandro delete that night?
qa.a: The whole bus-stop scene.

qa.q: What was Alejandro feeling as he listed his reasons to Noa?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and stung in his pride, so the comments landed like an attack and the excuses poured out.

qa.q: What could Alejandro try the next time Noa gives notes?
qa.a: Say "let me think about it" and write the comments down instead of answering at once, then read the page aloud later as he did at eleven.

qa.q: How might Noa see the new version handed over without a word?
qa.a: Noa probably feels quietly satisfied and amused, seeing the notes were used even though Alejandro argued with them the day before.

grounding: Shows a teenager who meets feedback with a stream of excuses and then quietly uses it in private, showing the reaction was pride rather than disagreement.
